newsitem.title: JAPAN: Renewed bank fears hit Japan stocks, yen bonds soar.
newsitem.headline: Renewed bank fears hit Japan stocks, yen bonds soar.

text.p: A fresh anxiety attack over the health of Japan's once-mighty banking sector dealt another blow to Japanese stocks on Monday, driving the key share index down two percent in jittery trade.
Sales of bank shares were triggered by a variety of vague rumours about new problems and possible large derivatives losses in some Japanese banks, brokers said.
"The bank shares' vulnerability to rumours proved that few investors preferred to buy those shares now," said Harushige Kobayashi, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities Co.

The talk raised concern about whether banks already struggling to tackle their bad loan problems will be able to survive in a more competitive environment when the government pushes through its "Big Bang" financial reforms, brokers said.

The benchmark Nikkei average of 225 leading shares shed 354.46 points or 2.00 percent to end the session at 17,334.90, after briefly dipping to 17,280.20. Its March futures finished 280 points lower at 17,380.
The banking sector was the top percentage loser on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange.

Adding to the sector's dark mood was a mid-afternoon announcement by Moody's Investors Service that it had lowered its ratings outlook for Nippon Credit Bank Ltd, Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd, Yasuda Trust & Banking and Chuo Trust & Banking to negative from stable.

The global credit agency said the downgraded banks had been having serious asset quality problems and their respective earnings, existing capital and reserves might not provide a sufficient cushion to absorb required loan-loss provisions.

Shares in Mitsubishi Trust & Banking Corp 8204.T were heavily sold on Monday, depressed by a downward revision of its earnings forecast late last week. The shares closed down 150 yen at 1,100 yen on heavy turnover of 2.39 million shares.
Vague rumours circulated in the yen bond market that Mitsubishi Trust may be suffering losses from derivatives trading, although a bank spokesman denied the rumour.
"We have found no evidence of this," the spokesman said.

The rumours helped to pull down long-term interest rates in the Japanese government bond market, because any further worsening in the health of Japan's financial sector would likely prevent the Japanese central bank from changing its ultra-low interest rate policy, traders said.
The key March bond futures hit a record high of 126.83 at one stage, but slipped off a bit to end 0.48 lower at 126.70.

The dollar, meanwhile, retained small gains and stayed at above 119 yen by late Tokyo trade. Trading was trapped between caution over a report of dollar-selling intervention on Friday and worries over the health of Japanese banks.
The dollar stood at around 119.20 yen in late trade in Tokyo, compared with Friday's New York close of around 118.90.
In other individual bank shares, Fuji Bank Ltd closed 120 yen lower at 1,180 yen, ranking as the seventh biggest loser. Shares in Chuo Trust & Banking Co Ltd lost 68 yen to finish at 722 yen.
Daiwa Bank Ltd lost 32 yen to end at 477 yen.
The prospect of fierce competition in the financial sector after Japan's planned "Big Bang" deregulation is also giving the stock market a negative undertone, brokers said.

Over the weekend, the influential director of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, Eisuke Sakakibara, said Japan's financial sector, especially banks, must be ready for major "bloodletting" after the planned "Big Bang" reforms.
